8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":16,"verseId":7,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Bondage and Liberation","totalVerses":10,"verseData":{"id":"v16_7","number":7,"title":"No Bound One Exists Prior to Binding","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"If prior to binding There is a bound one, There would be bondage, but there isn't. The rest has been explained by the gone, the not-gone, and the goer."},"philosophy":{"insight":"Temporal analysis of bondage: can the \"bound one\" exist BEFORE the binding? No — before binding occurs, there's no \"bound one\" (they're not bound yet). After binding, there would already be a bound one (redundant). During binding — the standard temporal trilemma applies. Nāgārjuna explicitly references Ch.2's analysis of motion: \"the rest has been explained.\"","madhyamaka":"The temporal analysis mirrors Ch.2 exactly: (1) Before binding: no \"bound one\" exists (nothing is bound yet). (2) After binding: already bound, so binding is redundant. (3) During binding: the being is simultaneously bound and not-bound (contradiction). The \"gone, not-gone, and goer\" (gatam, agatam, gantā) is a direct cross-reference to Ch.2's refutation of inherent motion.","quantum":"Temporal ordering in quantum mechanics: in quantum events, the strict temporal ordering of \"before/during/after\" can break down (delayed-choice experiments, retrocausality). The quantum world doesn't always respect the classical temporal sequence that the concept of \"prior to binding\" assumes.","bridge":"Both quantum temporal non-ordering and the Buddhist temporal trilemma challenge the assumption that processes have clean \"before/during/after\" phases. QM: temporal ordering is uncertain in some experiments. Buddhism: the \"before/during/after\" of binding can't inherently establish the bound one.","accessible":"Can you be a \"prisoner\" before you're imprisoned? No — you're free before imprisonment. Can you become a prisoner during imprisonment? You'd be both free and imprisoned at the same moment. After? You're already a prisoner. When exactly does imprisonment happen? The temporal analysis breaks down.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, beings become bound through grasping over time. Ultimately, the temporal mechanism of binding can't be inherently established — no \"moment of becoming bound\" can be pinpointed.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying bondage doesn't happen. It happens conventionally — as a dependent process. The point: no specific MOMENT of inherent becoming-bound can be identified. The process is gradual and dependent, not inherent."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Delayed-Choice Experiments — Temporal Ordering Breaks Down","score":61,"strength":"Medium","explanation":"In delayed-choice quantum experiments, the \"before/during/after\" sequence doesn't always apply as expected. Like the temporal trilemma of binding: the clean temporal ordering that inherent bondage requires isn't available.","caveat":"Delayed-choice experiments are specific QM setups. The parallel is about the breakdown of strict temporal ordering for inherent processes."},"animation":{"visualBridge":"A timeline with three segments: \"Before Binding\" (no bound one), \"During Binding\" (contradiction), \"After Binding\" (redundant). Each segment fails to locate the moment of inherent bondage.","educationalGoal":"User sees that no temporal moment can be identified where inherent bondage begins — the process is temporal but the inherent state can't be temporally located."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"What does \"the rest has been explained\" refer to?","a":"It's a direct cross-reference to Ch.2: \"Examination of Motion.\" Ch.2 showed that motion can't be found on the gone (past path), the not-gone (future path), or in the goer (present agent). V.7 says the same analysis applies to bondage — all temporal possibilities have been refuted.","realLifeExample":"A lawyer saying \"this case is identical to the one we already decided — see Case #2.\" Nāgārjuna is citing his own previous argument as precedent."},{"q":"Why can't the \"bound one\" exist before binding?","a":"Before binding occurs, the being is free (not yet bound). A free being isn't a \"bound one.\" For a \"bound one\" to exist before binding, they'd have to be bound before being bound — circular and incoherent.","realLifeExample":"Can someone be \"married\" before the wedding? No — before the ceremony, they're single. A \"married person\" can't exist before marriage occurs."},{"q":"Why can't binding happen \"during\" binding?","a":"During binding, the being is transitioning from free to bound. At that moment, they're both free (not yet bound) and bound (being bound) — a contradiction for inherent states. Inherently free and inherently bound can't coexist.","realLifeExample":"Can a glass be both empty and full at the same moment? During filling, it's transitioning — but it can't inherently be BOTH empty AND full simultaneously."},{"q":"How does this connect to the broader MMK strategy?","a":"The temporal trilemma (before/during/after) is one of the MMK's most powerful tools. It refutes motion (Ch.2), arising (Ch.7), bondage (Ch.16), and other processes. The same pattern works everywhere because the issue isn't the specific concept but inherent temporal processes in general.","realLifeExample":"A master key that opens every lock. The temporal trilemma is a \"master argument\" that works on any concept that involves temporal process — because inherent temporal processes are universally impossible."},{"q":"Does this mean processes don't happen in time?","a":"No — processes happen conventionally in time. We're born, age, and die in temporal sequence. But this temporal sequence can't be inherently established — there's no precise, inherent \"moment\" when free becomes bound, young becomes old, alive becomes dead. The transitions are gradual and dependent.","realLifeExample":"When exactly does a child become an adult? At 18? 21? There's no precise inherent moment — it's a gradual, conventional transition. The process happens; the inherent moment doesn't."},{"q":"How does v.7 advance from v.6?","a":"V.6 showed grasping doesn't inherently produce bondage (action ≠ state). V.7 adds temporal analysis: even if we grant the grasping-bondage connection, we can't locate the temporal moment when bondage begins. V.8 will add the final analysis: the paradox of release.","deeper":"V.7's explicit reference to Ch.2 is methodologically significant. It shows Nāgārjuna views his arguments as UNIVERSAL templates, not ad hoc refutations. The pattern that refuted motion in Ch.2 equally refutes bondage in Ch.16. This universality is what makes the MMK a systematic treatise rather than a collection of individual arguments."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"Why can't the \"bound one\" exist before binding?","options":["A) They can","B) Before binding occurs, the being is free — not yet bound.
